name: Brindisi Airport
before:
The airport for Brindisi and the Salento, 6 km from the city centre, and the obvious arrival for the heel of Italy. It also goes by Papola Casale and Salento Airport, so all three names turn up in supplier systems.

There is more going on here than the passenger traffic suggests. Since 1994 the airport has been the United Nations' main global logistics base for peacekeeping operations, taking over from Pisa, and since 2000 it has held the United Nations Humanitarian Response Depot, run by the World Food Programme, from which aid is sent to disaster zones worldwide. Its position in the Mediterranean and its road and port connections a few kilometres away also make it important to Italian defence and to NATO.

It began as a military airfield in the 1920s and only became legally a civilian airport in 2008, with the military side still operating under its own name.

Commercial flights to Rome date from the 1930s, and Alitalia took the route over after the Second World War.
after:
Brindisi's airport, a few kilometres from the city centre and the obvious arrival for the Salento and the heel of Italy. It is also listed as Brindisi Casale, so expect both names in supplier systems.

There is more going on here than the passenger traffic suggests. Since 1994 Brindisi has hosted the United Nations' logistics base, chosen for its airfield and harbour and now the UN Global Service Centre, which supports peace operations worldwide. The city also holds one of the hubs of the UN Humanitarian Response Depot, run by the World Food Programme, from which aid is sent to emergencies around the world.
